cards.lead: The water closet with a trapped drain
cards.name: Flushing toilet with an S-trap, London
cards.summary: Alexander Cumming's 1775 patent for a flushing toilet with an S-bend trap kept sewer gases out of buildings, and the trap remains in most toilets today.
cards.description: In 1775 Alexander Cumming, a watchmaker working in London, was granted the first patent for a flushing toilet with an S-shaped trap that held water in the waste pipe. About three years later Joseph Bramah patented a water closet with a hinged flap in place of the slide valve.
cards.origin_note: History Hit calls Cumming's 1775 patent the first for a flushing toilet with an S-trap, but the source does not rule out earlier trapped designs.

impact.note: Kept the lead's scores; the source reports the trap in most modern toilets but gives no measure of reach.

events.statement: Alexander Cumming was granted the first patent for a flushing toilet, with an S-trap to keep sewer gases out.
events.quote: In 1775, Alexander Cummings was awarded the first patent for a flushing version of the toilet.
events.locator: Section: He created an S-shaped plumbing design

events.label: c. 1778
events.statement: Joseph Bramah was awarded a new patent for a flushing toilet three years after Cumming's, replacing the slide valve with a hinged flap.
events.quote: Just three years later, a new patent was awarded to Joseph Bramah
events.locator: Section: He created an S-shaped plumbing design

sources.title: Alexander Cummings: The Scottish Pioneer of the Flush Toilet

cards.note: Smithsonian dates the first sale of Kotex pads to October 1919 in Chicago, not Birmingham in 1888. It also calls Lister's Towels possibly the first disposable option, so Kotex was not shown to be the first known.
cards.name: Kotex disposable sanitary pads, Chicago
cards.summary: Kotex pads, made from wartime Cellucotton wadding, were first sold as disposable sanitary pads in Chicago in October 1919.
cards.description: Kimberly-Clark adapted Cellucotton, a material first used in World War I hospitals as a bandage, into disposable sanitary pads. In October 1919 a Woolworth's store in Chicago sold the first box of Kotex pads, which the source says would appeal given the discomfort of cloth pads.
cards.origin_note: The source says Kotex began as a wartime invention, but also calls Lister's Towels possibly the first disposable option, so priority and independence are not settled.

impact.note: Kept the lead's scores; the source does not measure how widely disposable pads spread.

cards.why: The source says cloth pads were uncomfortable and inconvenient, and women were expected to work and attend school all month.

events.label: October 1919
events.statement: The first box of Kotex pads was sold at a Woolworth's department store in Chicago.
events.quote: In October 1919, the Woolworth’s department store in Chicago sold the first box of Kotex pads

sources.title: The Surprising Origins of Kotex Pads

open_questions: Check Lister's Towels and the 1888 Southall's product against primary sources; the lead's dates for them were not checked here.
Confirm where Kotex was manufactured (Neenah, Wisconsin, per other sources not opened here).

cards.note: The source dates the first documented public dissection to 1315 and describes it as the first in more than 1700 years. The 1543 end date was not checked in this batch, so only the 1315 event is recorded.
cards.name: Public human dissection at Bologna
cards.summary: Mondino de' Liuzzi's documented public dissection in 1315 restored human anatomy after more than 1,700 years and was the basis of his anatomy text.
cards.description: Mondino de' Liuzzi performed a documented public dissection in 1315, the first in more than 1700 years. His Anathomia combined the teachings of ancient anatomists with his own first-hand account of dissection.
cards.origin_note: The source says the 1315 dissection was the first documented public dissection in more than 1700 years, so it revived a practice that had lapsed.

impact.note: Kept the lead's scores; the source does not measure reach or later influence.

events.statement: Mondino de' Liuzzi performed the first documented public dissection in more than 1,700 years.
events.quote: In 1315, already a distinguished scientist and university professor, de’ Liuzzi performed the first documented public dissection in more than 1700 years

sources.title: Art in Science: Mondino de’ Liuzzi: The Restorer of Anatomy

open_questions: Check the 1543 end date (Vesalius, De humani corporis fabrica) against an opened source.

cards.note: The source supports a caesarean operation witnessed in 1879, but does not say the practice was independent or give its age, so the origin is set to unknown.
cards.name: Caesarean section in Bunyoro
cards.summary: Bunyoro doctors performed caesarean delivery under banana-wine anaesthesia in 1879, and mother and child both did well, as an observer recorded.
cards.description: In 1879 Robert Felkin, a British medical student, watched Bunyoro doctors deliver a child by caesarean section under banana-alcohol anaesthesia. The wound was closed with iron spikes and covered with cloth, and both mother and baby did well over the following days.
cards.origin_note: The source describes a well-codified surgical technique that suggests long experience, but it does not say whether the practice was independent of other surgery.

impact.note: Kept the lead's scores; the source reports no successors or spread beyond the observed kingdom.

events.statement: Robert Felkin, a British medical student, watched Bunyoro doctors perform a caesarean delivery under general anaesthesia.
events.quote: In 1879, during a missionary expedition in the actual Uganda, the British medical student Robert Felkin witnessed a cesarean delivery surgery under general anaesthesia

sources.title: Overview of surgical and anesthesia practice in sub-Saharan Africa during the 19th century: the example of the people of Bunyoro

open_questions: Felkin's original 1884 report was not opened; the secondary source names the Edinburgh Medical Journal without a year.

cards.note: The NLM exhibit dates Max Sänger's case for uterine sutures to 1882 at Leipzig. No fetched source supports a 1881 operation by Kehrer, and nothing shows the sutured operation was independent, so origin is unknown and reach is lowered from 3 to 2.
cards.name: Sutured caesarean section, Leipzig
cards.summary: Max Sänger of Leipzig made a strong case in 1882 for suturing the uterus after caesarean section, and surgeons began to change their practice.
cards.description: In 1882 Max Sänger of Leipzig argued for closing the uterus with sutures after a caesarean section. The National Library of Medicine exhibit says that his case led surgeons to change their practice.
cards.origin_note: The exhibit records Sänger's 1882 case but does not say whether German surgeons reached uterine suturing separately from others.

impact.note: Lowered reach from the lead's 3, because the claim that a fifth of the world's children are now born this way is not sourced here.

events.statement: Max Sänger of Leipzig made a strong case for uterine sutures, and surgeons began to change their practice.
events.quote: In 1882, Max Saumlnger, of Leipzig made such a strong case for uterine sutures that surgeons began to change their practice.

sources.title: Cesarean Section - A Brief History: Part 3

open_questions: Kehrer's 1881 operation at Meckesheim needs a primary source; the sources found were secondary and disagreed on the incision.

cards.lead: Positive-pressure ventilation and intensive care in Copenhagen
cards.note: The Smithsonian source says Ibsen read the 1950 Bower-Bennett positive-pressure report and used it in 1952, so the method was derived rather than first known. The 1953 ICU date was not verified in the fetched text.
cards.name: Positive-pressure ventilation via tracheostomy, Copenhagen
cards.summary: In the 1952 Copenhagen polio epidemic, Bjørn Ibsen's bag ventilation through a tracheostomy cut bulbar polio deaths to about 11 percent by March 1953.
cards.description: Bjørn Ibsen, an anaesthesiologist, bag-ventilated polio patients through tracheostomy tubes during the 1952 bulbar polio epidemic, after reading a 1950 positive-pressure report. By March 1953 only 11 percent of patients who developed bulbar polio had died.
cards.origin_note: Ibsen read the 1950 Bower-Bennett positive-pressure report and adapted it in Copenhagen in 1952, so the method was transmitted, not first known.

impact.note: Kept the lead's scores; the source describes ICUs and ventilators spreading but does not give shares of population.

cards.why: The Blegdam Hospital in Copenhagen was overwhelmed in August 1952, with one iron lung and hundreds of bulbar polio patients.

events.statement: Ibsen's bag ventilation through tracheostomy tubes became central to his answer to the 1952 bulbar polio crisis.
events.quote: this technique became a crucial element of Ibsen’s answer to the bulbar polio crisis of 1952

events.statement: Bulbar polio mortality in Copenhagen fell from 87 percent to about 50 percent in one week.
events.quote: In one week, the mortality of bulbar polio fell from 87 to barely 50 percent.

events.label: March 1953
events.statement: By March 1953 only 11 percent of patients who developed bulbar polio had died.
events.quote: As the embers of the Copenhagen outbreak cooled in March 1953, only 11 percent of patients who developed bulbar polio died.

sources.title: How a Polio Outbreak in Copenhagen Led to the Invention of the Ventilator

open_questions: The Copenhagen ICU opening date of 1953 (Kommunehospitalet) is not confirmed by the fetched text; Lassen's Lancet report was not opened.
Check the Bower-Bennett device date and place against a primary paper, since the source names them only briefly.
